The Full Stack Web Development internship in short

In the SkillMe Full Stack Web Development internship you build one of 3 projects, such as Modern Interactive Portfolio & DevStudio, a project where you build your own personal portfolio website with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and put it live on the internet by the end of the month. In week 1 you build a single-page portfolio with a header, an About section, a Projects section and a Contact section using only HTML and CSS. By week 4 you finish your portfolio with a validated contact form, fix accessibility issues, and deploy it for free so anyone can visit it. Each milestone is posted on LinkedIn and checked against that week's checklist before it counts. Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month.

One of 3 real projects, built over four weeks

You are assigned one of these projects when you start, and build it milestone by milestone.

Week by week

What each week of the Full Stack Web Development internship covers

Shown for Modern Interactive Portfolio & DevStudio. The other projects follow the same four-week shape.

  1. Week 1 of 4

    Your First Portfolio Page with HTML & CSS

    Beginner2-3 hours

    Build a single-page portfolio with a header, an About section, a Projects section and a Contact section using only HTML and CSS. This is the base you will keep improving every week, so focus on clean structure and simple, readable styling.

    What you learn

    • Semantic HTML tags like header, nav, main, section and footer
    • The CSS box model: margin, border, padding and content
    • Flexbox for laying out a navbar and rows of cards
    • Using CSS variables for colours and fonts so the design stays consistent

    What you submit

    • An index.html and style.css portfolio page with About, Projects and Contact sections
    • At least 3 styled project cards
    • A Git repository with at least 3 meaningful commits
    • A 30-60 second screen recording scrolling through the page
    How week 1 is reviewed
    • The page uses semantic tags (header, nav, main, section, footer) instead of only divs
    • Clicking each nav link scrolls to the matching section
    • Colours and fonts are defined once as CSS variables and reused
    • Every image has a meaningful alt attribute
    • The page has no broken images or console errors

    Stretch goal: Add a simple hover effect on project cards (a small lift with transform: translateY(-4px) and a transition).

  2. Week 2 of 4

    Responsive Layout & Project Cards with JavaScript

    Beginner+2-3 hours

    Make your portfolio look good on phones and start using JavaScript to control the page. You will add a mobile menu and generate your project cards from a JavaScript array, so adding a new project means editing data instead of copying HTML.

    What you learn

    • Media queries and a mobile-first approach to responsive design
    • Selecting elements and listening for events with querySelector and addEventListener
    • Storing data in an array of objects and rendering it to the page with a loop
    • Toggling CSS classes from JavaScript to show and hide things

    What you submit

    • A portfolio that works on mobile, tablet and desktop widths
    • A working mobile hamburger menu
    • Project cards generated from a JavaScript array with working filter buttons
    • A short demo video showing the page resizing and the filters in action
    How week 2 is reviewed
    • There is no horizontal scrolling at 375px width
    • The hamburger menu opens and closes on small screens and is hidden on desktop
    • Adding a new object to the projects array makes a new card appear without touching HTML
    • Clicking a filter button shows only matching projects, and All shows every project
    • The browser console shows no errors

    Stretch goal: Highlight the active filter button and close the mobile menu automatically when a nav link is clicked.

  3. Week 3 of 4

    Live GitHub Repos & Dark Mode

    Intermediate2-3 hours

    Connect your portfolio to real data by fetching your public repositories from the GitHub API and showing them on the page. You will also add a dark mode toggle that remembers the visitor's choice using localStorage.

    What you learn

    • Fetching data from a public API with fetch and async/await
    • Handling loading and error states so the page never looks broken
    • Saving and reading small settings with localStorage
    • Theming a site by swapping CSS variables with a class on body

    What you submit

    • A GitHub Repos section populated live from the GitHub REST API
    • Visible loading and error states for the repos section
    • A dark mode toggle that is remembered after a page refresh
    • A demo video showing repos loading and the theme switching
    How week 3 is reviewed
    • The repos section shows at least 5 of your real public repositories
    • A 'Loading...' message appears before data arrives and is removed afterwards
    • If the fetch fails, a readable error message is shown instead of a blank section
    • Refreshing the page keeps the theme the visitor last selected
    • Both themes are readable with good text contrast

    Stretch goal: Add a language filter dropdown built from the unique language values in your repos.

  4. Week 4 of 4

    Contact Form, Accessibility & Going Live

    Intermediate+2-3 hours

    Finish your portfolio with a validated contact form, fix accessibility issues, and deploy it for free so anyone can visit it. By the end you will have a real link to put on your resume and LinkedIn profile.

    What you learn

    • Client-side form validation with JavaScript and helpful error messages
    • Basic accessibility: labels, keyboard navigation, focus styles and colour contrast
    • Auditing a page with Lighthouse and fixing what it reports
    • Deploying a static site to GitHub Pages or Netlify

    What you submit

    • A contact form with client-side validation and clear error messages
    • A Lighthouse report screenshot with an accessibility score of 90 or higher
    • A public live URL for your portfolio
    • A README with a screenshot, live link and feature list
    How week 4 is reviewed
    • Submitting the form with empty or invalid fields shows specific error messages and does not reset the form
    • Every interactive element can be reached and used with the keyboard alone
    • Lighthouse accessibility score is 90 or above
    • The live URL loads correctly on both desktop and mobile
    • The README includes the live link and at least one screenshot

    Stretch goal: Connect the form to a free form service like Formspree so messages actually reach your inbox.

Is it for you?

Who the Full Stack Web Development internship is for, and what you leave with

This internship fits you if

  • You know the basics of HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript and want a real project to show for it, not more tutorials.
  • You can start at beginner level. Week 1: Build a single-page portfolio with a header, an About section, a Projects section and a Contact section using only HTML and CSS.
  • You want to reach intermediate+ level in four weeks. Week 4: Finish your portfolio with a validated contact form, fix accessibility issues, and deploy it for free so anyone can visit it.
  • You can give it about 2-3 hours a week around college or a job, from any country.

Full Stack Web Development internship: questions and answers

What will I build in the Full Stack Web Development internship?

You are assigned one of 3 projects: Modern Interactive Portfolio & DevStudio, TaskFlow: Collaborative Sprint & Kanban Workspace or WeatherNow: City Weather Dashboard. Each is a single project built up over four weekly milestones, so each week adds to the last.

What skills will I learn in the Full Stack Web Development internship?

The Full Stack Web Development internship works with HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript. Week 1: semantic HTML tags like header, nav, main, section and footer; the CSS box model: margin, border, padding and content. Week 2: media queries and a mobile-first approach to responsive design; selecting elements and listening for events with querySelector and addEventListener. Week 3: fetching data from a public API with fetch and async/await; handling loading and error states so the page never looks broken. Week 4: client-side form validation with JavaScript and helpful error messages; basic accessibility: labels, keyboard navigation, focus styles and colour contrast.

Do I need experience to apply for the Full Stack Web Development internship?

You need the basics of HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript, not prior internship experience. Week 1 starts at beginner level, where you build a single-page portfolio with a header, an About section, a Projects section and a Contact section using only HTML and CSS. Week 4 reaches intermediate+ level. A short screening quiz (8 questions, about 5 minutes) checks you are ready to start.

How is each Full Stack Web Development milestone reviewed?

Every week has a checklist, and a milestone is approved only when it meets all of it. For week 1 of Modern Interactive Portfolio & DevStudio, that means: the page uses semantic tags (header, nav, main, section, footer) instead of only divs; clicking each nav link scrolls to the matching section; colours and fonts are defined once as CSS variables and reused; every image has a meaningful alt attribute; the page has no broken images or console errors. Reviewers include engineers who work at Walmart, Google and LinkedIn, and work that misses the bar comes back with notes.

What can I put on my resume after the Full Stack Web Development internship?

Each approved milestone gives you a line you can back up with a public LinkedIn post: Built my personal portfolio website from scratch using semantic HTML and CSS; Designed a clean layout with flexbox and a consistent colour theme using CSS variables; Structured the page into About, Projects and Contact sections with smooth in-page navigation; Made my portfolio fully responsive using media queries and a mobile-first approach; Built a mobile hamburger menu with vanilla JavaScript and DOM events; Rendered project cards dynamically from a JavaScript array with category filters; Integrated the GitHub REST API into my portfolio using fetch and async/await; Added loading and error handling so the page stays friendly when the network fails; Built a dark mode toggle that remembers the user's preference with localStorage; Deployed my personal portfolio live and shared it as my online resume; Built a contact form with client-side validation and accessible error messages; Improved accessibility to a 90+ Lighthouse score with keyboard support and better contrast.

What are the other projects in the Full Stack Web Development internship?

TaskFlow: Collaborative Sprint & Kanban Workspace: Build a simple Kanban board (To Do, In Progress, Done) that runs in your browser and remembers your tasks. WeatherNow: City Weather Dashboard: Build a weather dashboard where you search any city and see the current weather and a 7-day forecast, using a free public API. Every project follows the same four-week shape, with one reviewed milestone a week.

Is the Full Stack Web Development internship paid? Is there a stipend?

Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month. It is performance-based: 8–10 interns are picked each month from those who complete the internship and hold an issued certificate. It is not paid to every intern.

How much time does it take?

4 weeks, one milestone a week, each planned for about 2-3 hours. It is fully remote and open worldwide, so you work around college or a job.
